title: The Morning UT Bank's Staff Found the Doors Locked in Accra
dek: In August 2017 Ghana's central bank closed the bank Prince Kofi Amoabeng had built, and the two sides have disputed why ever since.

story.event: The Bank of Ghana's revocation of UT Bank's licence and the disputed account of its collapse
story.summary: On 14 August 2017 the Bank of Ghana revoked the licences of UT Bank and Capital Bank, calling them deeply insolvent, appointed PwC as receiver and transferred their deposits and selected assets to GCB Bank. UT's founder, Prince Kofi Amoabeng, who says he had stepped down as chief executive in 2015, has argued that the bank could have been rescued more cheaply while also saying UT must take the blame first; criminal charges filed in 2020 against him, UT Holdings and others remained before the High Court in early 2026, after charges against a former deputy governor were withdrawn in January 2025.
paragraphs: On Monday morning, 14 August 2017, staff arriving at UT Bank's head office near Accra's airport found themselves locked out, with police at the doors. The Bank of Ghana had revoked the licences of UT Bank and Capital Bank, appointed PwC as receiver and moved all their deposits and selected assets to the state-owned GCB Bank, whose name the branches would carry when they reopened that afternoon. No depositor, the governor said, would lose money.

Prince Kofi Amoabeng, a retired army captain, had built UT over twenty years into a group with a listed bank. He says he stepped down as the bank's chief executive in 2015, though he remained head of its parent group, UT Holdings. The central bank called both banks deeply insolvent and said their owners had repeatedly agreed plans to restore capital without raising it. Provisional figures put UT's liabilities at GH¢850 million against assets of GH¢112 million. The governor, Ernest Addison, later said 44 per cent of its loans were non-performing and that a would-be buyer had found it too risky to take on.

Amoabeng has told it differently. In 2019 he said investors had been ready with proposals, and that writing off part of what UT owed would have cost far less than a closure he put at GH¢2.2 billion; by 2025 he was calling it politically influenced. He also said UT had run itself down and "must take the blame first." Addison called the shareholders' request that the state carry the cost of UT's bad loans "preposterous". A year after the closure Amoabeng wrote that his heart bled, and that what mattered most to him was staff left with little to show for years of service.

The courts have not settled it. In February 2020 the state replaced its first charges against him, of stealing and money laundering, with 42 counts in the High Court, including fraudulent breach of trust, against Amoabeng, UT Holdings, two former central bank officials and others. They pleaded not guilty. In January 2025 the new attorney-general withdrew the charges against one of those officials, the former deputy governor Johnson Asiama, while the trial of the others was to continue. In January 2026 Amoabeng said he had been in court for almost eight years.

quote.text: "Do not find fault with me", answered vitality, "Many a time a censurer himself is reproved, while the censured is found faultless. How do you know that I have forced the hand?
quote.locator: "Human Freedom and Responsibility", The Allegory of the Pen
quote.source_title: Some Religious and Moral Teachings of Al-Ghazzali, tr. Syed Nawab Ali, Project Gutenberg eBook #73140
quote.connection: In al-Ghazali's allegory a devotee asks the paper, the ink, the pen and the hand who is to blame, and each points further along, warning that the accuser may be the one at fault. Around UT Bank, regulator and owner each point at the other, and no court has yet decided.

reflection: When something fails in public, everyone involved is under pressure to produce a clean account, and most clean accounts place the fault somewhere else. This story does not give you one. The regulator's figures are serious, and so is Amoabeng's claim that a cheaper rescue was turned down. Even his own account holds both: a rescue refused, and a company that had run itself down.

You will meet smaller versions of this: a project that stalls, a result that goes wrong, a falling-out between people you respect. It is possible to hold two accounts at once without deciding too early, and to begin with the part that was yours.
invitation: Think of one disagreement at work where you have heard only one side clearly. Today, ask the other person one open question about how it looked to them, and listen without replying.

sources.title: UT, Capital Bank collapse: We had no choice – BoG (14 August 2017)
sources.supports: The Bank of Ghana's statement that UT Bank and Capital Bank were 'deeply insolvent', their liabilities overwhelming their assets; repeated agreements on action plans and the owners' inability to raise capital; the Purchase and Assumption transaction with GCB Bank; UT Bank workers locked out of the head office at Airport on the Monday morning with police deployed; expectations on staff retention by GCB and the receiver.

sources.title: UT, Capital Bank insolvency: BoG to punish persons found culpable (14 August 2017)
sources.supports: Governor Ernest Addison's statement: restructuring and capital restoration plans found unacceptable; GCB chosen from a pool of bidders; 'no depositor will lose his or her funds'; investigation of shareholders, directors and management to follow.

sources.title: GCB Bank takes over distressed UT and Capital banks (14 August 2017)
sources.supports: Licences revoked for severe impairment of capital; PwC's Vish Ashiagbor and Eric Nana Nipah appointed receivers; all deposits and selected assets transferred to GCB; branches reopening at 1pm that Monday as GCB branches.

sources.title: 'My heart bleeds' over collapse of 20-year-old business – Amoabeng (August 2018)
sources.supports: Amoabeng's first public statement, a year after the closure: 'my heart bleeds'; the organisation built over 20 years; silence while EOCO investigated; his denial of the reported undisclosed GH¢5 million loan payment, which he said was the proceeds of selling his house; his description as a former army officer.

sources.title: UT Bank collapse affecting my other businesses – Kofi Amoabeng (17 August 2018)
sources.supports: Amoabeng as group CEO of UT Holdings; his regret that staff were left with little or nothing to show for years of service; difficulties servicing payments due to investors in the remaining group companies; the BoG-commissioned report's findings on related-party lending and governance.

sources.title: UT Bank could've survived if BoG had given us time – Kofi Amoabeng (9 February 2019)
sources.supports: Amoabeng's account: investors ready with proposals; owing about GH¢800 million against a closure costing at least GH¢2.2 billion; admission of corporate governance problems; 'We had run our company down' and 'UT must take the blame first'; no grudges.

sources.title: Shareholders asking gov't to shoulder cost of UT Bank's bad loans 'preposterous' – BoG Governor (16 January 2020)
sources.supports: Addison's account at the New Year School: the shareholders' request that the state bear the cost of bad loans was 'preposterous'; meetings with shareholders and directors; a potential acquirer finding UT 'highly unattractive and risky'; non-performing loans of 44 per cent; no corporate tax returns since 2015; the state guaranteeing depositors' funds.

sources.title: Defunct UT Bank's Kofi Amoabeng charged with stealing, money laundering (January 2020)
sources.supports: The first charges at an Accra circuit court; the Bank of Ghana's provisional figures of GH¢850 million in liabilities and GH¢112 million in assets; the receiver's suit against UT Holdings for over GH¢100 million.

sources.title: Defunct UT Bank boss faces 42 fresh charges (February 2020)
sources.supports: Discharge on the original stealing and money laundering charges and re-arraignment at the High Court on 42 charges, including fraudulent breach of trust, deceit of a public officer and fabrication of evidence, with five others including former deputy governor Johnson Asiama; the prosecution's allegations as set out in the charge sheet.

sources.title: We are not guilty – Duffuor, Asiama, Amoabeng, others deny collapsing banks (13 February 2020)
sources.supports: The accused in the UT Bank and uniBank cases pleading not guilty at the High Court.

sources.title: Attorney-General withdraws charges against former Deputy BoG Governor Johnson Asiama (30 January 2025)
sources.supports: Attorney-General Dominic Ayine's notice withdrawing all charges against Asiama in the uniBank and UT Bank cases; his co-accused in the UT case (Amoabeng, Raymond Amanfu, UT Holdings, Catherine Johnson, Robert Kwesi Armah); the withdrawal applying only to Asiama, with the trials of the others expected to proceed.

sources.title: Attorney-General files to withdraw charges against former Deputy Governor of BoG, Johnson Asiama (January 2025)
sources.supports: Second report of the January 2025 withdrawal for Asiama only, with the trials of the other accused expected to proceed.

sources.title: Political influence led to UT Bank's closure – Prince Kofi Amoabeng (20 January 2025)
sources.supports: Amoabeng's claim on JoyNews that there was political influence in the closure and that the clean-up was done haphazardly, while accepting the government's power to decide.

sources.title: I resigned before UT Bank collapse, yet faced eight years in court – Amoabeng (19 January 2026)
sources.supports: Amoabeng's statement that he resigned as CEO in 2015, two years before the collapse; that he had faced 'baseless charges' and had been in court for almost eight years, paying legal fees.

sources.title: Amoabeng, Duffour petition Parliament to probe BoG, GSE over banking sector clean-up (March 2021)
sources.supports: The Bank of Ghana's position that UT was insolvent and unable to recapitalise despite shareholders' assurances; Amoabeng's petition alleging revocation and delisting without administrative justice and seeking restoration of the licence.

sources.title: Collapsing UT Bank was a wrong decision – Kofi Amoabeng (20 February 2023)
sources.supports: Amoabeng's view that the closure was wrong and that the GH¢2.2 billion could have funded a supervised restructuring; 'I wasn't even the CEO at the time'; his description as a retired captain and founder.

cross_checks.claim: On 14 August 2017 the Bank of Ghana revoked UT Bank's licence and transferred its deposits and selected assets to GCB Bank
The Bank of Ghana said UT was insolvent and its owners had failed to recapitalise despite agreed plans
Amoabeng has argued the closure was wrong and that a cheaper rescue was possible
Amoabeng says he stepped down as UT Bank's chief executive in 2015
In February 2020 the state brought 42 charges at the High Court against Amoabeng and five others, who pleaded not guilty
In January 2025 the Attorney-General withdrew the charges against Johnson Asiama only, with the trial of the others to proceed

research_notes: Blame is disputed and is attributed throughout. The Bank of Ghana's case (statement of 14 August 2017 as reported by Citi FM; Governor Addison's New Year School speech, January 2020) is that UT was deeply insolvent, that its owners repeatedly agreed but failed to restore capital, that its plans were unacceptable, that 44 per cent of loans were non-performing and that a potential acquirer found it too risky. Amoabeng's case (Citi 2019 and 2023; JoyNews 2025; GhanaWeb 2026) is that investors had proposals, that a supervised restructuring would have cost less than the closure, that the clean-up was haphazard and politically influenced, and that he had resigned as chief executive in 2015; he has also said UT ran itself down and 'must take the blame first'. Court findings: no court has ruled on guilt or on the revocation in any source found. The circuit court discharged him in February 2020 only because the state withdrew the first charges in order to file 42 counts at the High Court; all accused pleaded not guilty; on 29-30 January 2025 the Attorney-General withdrew charges against Johnson Asiama alone, and Graphic and MyJoyOnline reported that the other trials were expected to proceed; in January 2026 Amoabeng said he had been in court for almost eight years. No verdict had been reported in any source found as of this research, so the story does not say the case has ended. The receiver's civil claim of over GH¢100 million against UT Holdings is mentioned in Citi (2020), but no outcome was found and it is not in the story. The prosecution's specific allegations (for example the escrow account and transfers of client investments to UT Holdings, as set out by 3News from the charge sheet) are allegations, not findings, and are left out of the story. Figures: BoG's provisional figures give UT's liabilities as GH¢850 million and assets as GH¢112 million; Amoabeng says UT owed about GH¢800 million and that the closure cost at least GH¢2.2 billion; Citi (2018) reports combined liquidity support to UT and Capital of over GH¢1.4 billion; 3News quotes the charge sheet as saying a GH¢650 million request in 2016 led to '$460 million' being released, apparently a cedi figure mistyped. The story uses only the BoG's provisional figures and Amoabeng's GH¢2.2 billion, each attributed. Amoabeng's role in 2017: he says he resigned as CEO in 2015; Citi described him in 2018 as group CEO of UT Holdings and in 2019 as President of UT Holdings, while a 2018 Citi headline still called him CEO of the bank; the story says he says he stepped down and remained head of the parent group. The founding date is given only as 'over twenty years', from Amoabeng's 2018 statement. The company field is given as 'UT Bank' rather than 'UT Bank (UT Holdings group)' because the repeat screen matched the shared company word 'Holdings' with Shoprite Holdings (Whitey Basson, 2016), a different company. The Bank of Ghana's own press release was not found at a working URL, so its words are taken from contemporary reports. Al-Ghazali's allegory, from the section on human freedom and responsibility, is about where agency lies; it is applied by analogy and the connection takes no side.
